messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 57

She is a 37-year-old Latin American woman who has spent most of her adult life working her way up in hospitality, and she speaks about that history with a mix of pride and exhaustion. As a hotel manager, she is used to being the one who stays calm when something goes wrong, the one who knows where the spare keys are, who can soothe an upset guest, who can walk into a room and quickly assess what needs to be handled. That competence has become part of how she understands herself. Before the assault, she describes herself as organized, energetic, and “good in a crisis.”

The assault occurs after a work-related evening that runs later than planned. She has stayed behind to deal with a staffing problem and then goes out with a colleague and a few others for a drink to mark the end of a difficult week. She trusts the people around her and does not think she is in danger. On the way home, she is sexually assaulted. In the aftermath, she remembers pieces in a way that feels jagged and humiliating: the sensation of freezing, the sound of her own breathing, the confusion of trying to understand what is happening while also wanting it to stop and wanting it to be over. What stays with her most is not only fear but the sharp collapse of her sense that she can read a situation correctly. She says that afterward she keeps thinking, again and again, “How did I not see it coming?”

In the days that follow, she functions on automatic. She goes to work because she cannot imagine not going, and because the hotel still needs her. She smiles at guests, handles complaints, checks schedules, and answers emails, but internally she feels split from herself, as if part of her is performing a familiar role while another part remains trapped in the event. She finds that ordinary sounds can send a jolt through her body. A room door closing too hard, footsteps behind her in a hallway, the buzz of an elevator, even the rustle of a man’s jacket near her in an enclosed space can make her muscles go rigid before she has time to think. She becomes more aware of exits than she ever used to be. In meetings, she positions herself near the door. When she walks through the hotel at night, she scans corners and mirrors, and she notices how much energy goes into simply feeling prepared.

Sleep changes quickly. She falls asleep exhausted and wakes up tense, sometimes from dreams she cannot fully remember but that leave her with the physical sensation of having been chased or held down. In the morning she feels as if she has not rested at all. She starts delaying bedtime because she dreads the return of that helpless feeling in the dark. During the day she has flashes that arrive without warning: a flash of light on a street, the smell of alcohol, the sight of a man’s hand on a door handle. These moments are brief, but they leave her shaky and angry with herself. She dislikes how often she feels caught off guard, especially because her job depends on being able to anticipate problems.

Over time, she becomes increasingly guarded with other people. She still lives with her partner, but she finds it hard to explain what she needs without feeling embarrassed or “difficult.” She wants comfort and also wants distance. Some evenings she sits beside him but barely speaks, then later feels guilty for seeming cold. Intimacy has become complicated; she sometimes dissociates during physical contact and then feels ashamed that her mind goes blank. She does not talk easily about the assault, even with people she trusts, because once she starts to describe it she worries she will lose control or make others uncomfortable. Instead, she carries it privately and puts on a competent face.

At work, the strain shows in subtler ways. She becomes less patient with minor problems, and her concentration slips when she is tired. She double-checks locks and security footage more than before. She has started taking longer routes through the hotel if it means she can avoid being alone in certain corridors. She thinks carefully about how guests are dressed, how they stand, who is lingering near the lobby, and she dislikes how quickly her attention turns toward threat. She misses the ease she once had with people and places. Even on good days, there is a persistent sense that the world is less predictable than she believed.

She still tries to keep up appearances, and many colleagues would describe her as capable and polished. But in quieter moments, she feels changed in ways that are hard to name: more tired, more alert, less able to relax into safety. She moves through her days carrying the memory of the assault alongside her usual responsibilities, and the effort of holding both seems to take more out of her than anyone at work can see.
